subject: physics

items.q: Which statement best describes the colours of the visible light spectrum?
items.correct: Each colour has its own narrow band of wavelength and frequency
items.misconception: Each colour has one exact wavelength and one exact frequency
items.why: Spectrum diagrams print a single figure beside each colour, and exam questions often say 'red light of wavelength 700 nm', which makes a colour look like one fixed number. Take the specification wording literally: each colour has a narrow band of wavelength and a narrow band of frequency. The bands sit side by side and run into one another, which is why the visible spectrum has no gaps in it.
items.random_wrong: Each colour has its own wavelength but all share one frequency

items.q: Red light and violet light both lie within the visible spectrum. Which statement about their bands is correct?
items.correct: The red band has longer wavelengths, so it has lower frequencies
items.misconception: The red band lies at one fixed wavelength and the violet at another
items.why: Spectrum diagrams print a single figure beside each colour, and exam questions often say 'red light of wavelength 700 nm', which makes a colour look like one fixed number. Take the specification wording literally: each colour has a narrow band of wavelength and a narrow band of frequency. The bands sit side by side and run into one another, which is why the visible spectrum has no gaps in it.
items.random_wrong: The red band has longer wavelengths but the same frequency

items.q: What is the difference between specular reflection and diffuse reflection?
items.correct: Specular reflection is from a smooth surface, diffuse from a rough one
items.misconception: Specular reflection is from a rough surface, and diffuse from a smooth one
items.why: Both words are unfamiliar and neither sounds obviously like 'mirror' or 'scattered', so students memorise the pair without a hook and then attach them the wrong way round. Link 'specular' to 'spectacles' and 'speculum', both to do with mirrors: specular means mirror-like, from a smooth surface. Diffuse shares its root with 'diffused', meaning spread out — the scattering case.
items.random_wrong: Specular reflection always obeys the law of reflection and diffuse does not

items.q: A mirror shows a clear image of a lamp, but a sheet of white paper beside it looks equally bright from every direction. Why does the paper behave differently?
items.correct: Its rough surface scatters light into many directions
items.misconception: Its rough surface obeys no law, so the rays leave at random angles
items.why: The scattered ray diagram looks disordered, and students assume that disorder in the picture means the rule has broken down. Draw the normal at each separate point on a bumpy surface. Each normal points a different way, but at every point the angle of incidence still equals the angle of reflection. The rule holds; only the surface has changed.
items.random_wrong: Its rough surface takes in the light and gives it out slowly

items.q: How does a colour filter work?
items.correct: It absorbs certain wavelengths of light and transmits the others
items.misconception: It reflects the unwanted wavelengths and lets the rest through
items.why: Students transfer the rule for opaque coloured objects, where the colours you do not see are the ones sent back, to a transparent filter without adjusting it. The specification says filters work by absorbing certain wavelengths and transmitting others. Hold a green filter up to a bright lamp: the room behind the lamp does not gain a red glow, because the red is taken in, not sent back.
items.random_wrong: It adds its own colour to the white light that passes through

items.q: White light is shone through a blue filter. What emerges from the filter, and why?
items.correct: Blue light, because the other wavelengths are absorbed by it
items.misconception: White light that has been dyed blue as it travelled through
items.why: The filter is visibly coloured and the emerging light matches it, so 'the filter coloured the light' looks like the obvious explanation. Shine pure blue light through a red filter and almost nothing comes out. If the filter were adding red, red would appear. Instead the blue is absorbed and there is no red for the filter to transmit.
items.random_wrong: All the colours, but with the blue much brighter than the rest

items.q: What determines the colour of an opaque object viewed in white light?
items.correct: The wavelengths that the object reflects most strongly
items.misconception: The wavelengths that the object absorbs most strongly of all
items.why: Students remember that colour involves both absorption and reflection but not which of the two reaches the eye, and 'the object takes in red, so it is red' sounds reasonable. Only light that reaches your eye can be seen. The colour you see is the light coming off the object, so it must be made of the reflected wavelengths. The absorbed ones never reach you at all.
items.random_wrong: The wavelengths that the object gives out when it is warm

items.q: A jumper appears white when it is lit by white light. What is happening to the light that falls on it?
items.correct: All wavelengths are reflected equally
items.misconception: All wavelengths are absorbed equally by it
items.why: Students associate white with emptiness and black with 'full', or they recall that black objects get hot and reason that being hot means the energy is coming back out. A black car roof gets far hotter in sunlight than a white one, because the black surface absorbs the energy instead of reflecting it. Reflecting every wavelength equally is what makes a surface look white.
items.random_wrong: All wavelengths pass straight through the wool

items.q: A piece of card looks black in a brightly lit room. Which explanation is correct?
items.correct: The card absorbs all of the wavelengths of light that fall on it
items.misconception: The light passes straight through the card without stopping
items.why: Students know that no light is coming back and jump to 'the light went somewhere else' — through the object — rather than accepting that the energy was taken in. Black objects here are opaque, so no light gets through. Hold a black card in front of a lamp and nothing shows through on the far side. The energy is absorbed and warms the card.
items.random_wrong: The card reflects every wavelength that falls upon it equally

items.q: Which statement is true of objects that transmit light?
items.correct: They are either transparent or translucent
items.misconception: They must be colourless as well as see-through
items.why: 'See-through' is learned as meaning colourless, so a coloured sheet gets filed with solid objects rather than with transmitting ones. A red filter is coloured and you can still see a lamp through it. Being coloured tells you which wavelengths are absorbed, not whether any light gets through at all.
items.random_wrong: They transmit light only when very smooth

items.q: Frosted bathroom glass lets light into the room, but no clear image can be seen through it. How is the glass best described?
items.correct: Translucent, since it scatters the light passing through
items.misconception: Transparent, since the light gets through the glass easily
items.why: The two words look and sound alike and both describe materials you can see light coming through, so students treat them as interchangeable. The test is the image, not the light. Transparent means you see a clear image through the material; translucent means light gets through but the image does not. Both transmit light, which is why the specification pairs them.
items.random_wrong: Opaque, since there is no clear image to be seen through it

items.q: A book cover appears red in white light. Which explanation of its colour is correct?
items.correct: Red is reflected and the other wavelengths absorbed
items.misconception: Red is absorbed by the cover and other wavelengths reflected
items.why: Students remember that colour involves both absorption and reflection but not which of the two reaches the eye, and 'the object takes in red, so it is red' sounds reasonable. Only light that reaches your eye can be seen. The colour you see is the light coming off the object, so it must be made of the reflected wavelengths. The absorbed ones never reach you at all.
items.random_wrong: Red is transmitted through the cover and the rest reflected

items.q: In white light a leaf looks green and a daisy petal looks white. Which explanation accounts for both?
items.correct: The leaf reflects green strongly and absorbs the other wavelengths; the petal reflects them all equally
items.misconception: The leaf absorbs green strongly and reflects the other wavelengths; the petal absorbs the whole range
items.why: Students remember that colour involves both absorption and reflection but not which of the two reaches the eye, and 'the object takes in red, so it is red' sounds reasonable. Only light that reaches your eye can be seen. The colour you see is the light coming off the object, so it must be made of the reflected wavelengths. The absorbed ones never reach you at all.
items.random_wrong: The leaf reflects green and absorbs the others; the petal absorbs every wavelength equally

items.q: A red counter is viewed through a green filter in white light. How does the counter appear?
items.correct: Black, because the filter absorbs the red light it reflects
items.misconception: Green, because the filter turns the light green as it passes
items.why: Everything seen through a coloured filter has a colour cast, so students generalise to 'the filter makes everything its own colour'. The filter can only transmit wavelengths that reach it. A red object sends only red towards the green filter, and the green filter absorbs red, so no light gets through and the object looks black.
items.random_wrong: Red, because the reflected light still gets through it

items.q: White light is passed through a red filter and then through a blue filter. What is seen after the second filter?
items.correct: Almost no light: each filter absorbs what the other passes
items.misconception: White light, because the second filter cancels the first out
items.why: Students carry over the rules for mixing coloured paints or adding coloured light beams, where combining two colours makes a new colour. Filters act one after the other, and each one only ever subtracts. Track the light through in order: white light in, red only after the first filter, then nothing after a filter that absorbs red.
items.random_wrong: Purple light, because the red and the blue light add together

items.q: A blue mug is placed in a darkroom lit only by red light. How does the mug appear?
items.correct: Black, as there is no blue light for it to reflect
items.misconception: Purple, since the red light mixes with the mug's own blue
items.why: Objects appear to 'have' their colour permanently, so students treat the colour as something the object emits rather than something it does to the incoming light. Take the light away and the colour disappears — a red jumper is invisible in a dark room. Colour depends on the light falling on the object, which is why objects change appearance under coloured lighting.
items.random_wrong: Blue, since the mug keeps its colour in any lighting

items.q: Do all the colours of visible light have the same frequency?
items.correct: Each colour has its own band of frequency as well as its own band of wavelength; red light has the lowest frequencies and violet the highest.
items.misconception: All visible light travels at the same speed, so all colours must share the same frequency and only the wavelength changes.
items.why: Students learn that all electromagnetic waves travel at the same speed in a vacuum and over-extend 'the same' from speed to frequency. Wave speed = frequency × wavelength. If the speed is fixed and the wavelength changes from colour to colour, then the frequency must change too — in the opposite direction.
items.note: no MCQ covers this misconception, so no third distractor was authored for it; none invented

items.q: Does a rough surface such as paper reflect the light that falls on it?
items.correct: Yes. A rough surface reflects light, but the reflection is diffuse: the light is scattered in many directions.
items.misconception: Rough or dull surfaces absorb light rather than reflecting it, and only shiny surfaces reflect.
items.why: Students equate 'reflective' with 'shiny', so a matt surface reads as one that does not reflect at all. You can see a sheet of white paper from every side of the room, which is only possible because it is reflecting light towards you from every angle. If it absorbed the light it would look black.
items.note: no MCQ covers this misconception, so no third distractor was authored for it; none invented

items.q: Is the colour of an opaque object set by the light it lets through?
items.correct: No. An opaque object transmits no light; its colour is set by which wavelengths it reflects most strongly.
items.misconception: Objects are coloured because certain wavelengths pass through them, as happens with a filter.
items.why: Filters and coloured objects are taught close together, so the transmission explanation gets applied to solid objects as well. Sort the situation first. If light gets through, the object is transparent or translucent and transmission matters. If the object is opaque, only reflection and absorption are available.
items.note: no MCQ covers this misconception, so no third distractor was authored for it; none invented

items.q: A material lets light through but you cannot see a clear image. Is it opaque?
items.correct: No, it is translucent. Opaque means that no light is transmitted at all.
items.misconception: Anything you cannot see a clear image through counts as opaque.
items.why: Students use 'can I see through it?' as the single test and treat a blurred view as no view, which lumps translucent materials in with opaque ones. Use two tests, not one. First, does any light get through? If not, it is opaque. If light does get through, ask whether the image is clear: clear means transparent, blurred means translucent.
items.note: no MCQ covers this misconception, so no third distractor was authored for it; none invented
